rows.claim: defendant A: rotating the board 90 degrees clockwise and renaming the direction keys with it (up->right->down->left->up) preserves the game exactly -- the direction keys are bound to board coordinates, so the true symmetry carries its own key renaming; declared under the explicit caliber with per-element action maps

defendant B: the same 90-degree rotation with the direction keys PINNED (up must stay up) -- the naive-intuition claim that 'the board looks the same rotated', filed deliberately under the fixed caliber to show it is the key renaming, not the state permutation, that makes defendant A true

defendant C: mirroring the board top-bottom and swapping the vertical keys with it (up<->down, left/right unchanged) preserves the game -- the second generator of the 8-element board group, declared explicit with per-element action maps

defendant D: the FULL 8-element board symmetry group D4 (identity, three rotations, four reflections), each element carrying its own direction-key renaming -- the complete non-trivial positive control; the compression reading is the orbit count

control: mirror the top row only (cells 0<->1 swap, bottom row untouched) -- the board looks locally mirror-symmetric but this map moves one cell pair off the square's symmetry group; filed under fixed and expected to be refused

positive control: padding states 3 and 11 have byte-identical rows (every action self-loops, reward 0), so the swap is a genuine symmetry under the pinned-key reading and should be admitted everywhere
